title: Squares of a Sorted Array
description: Brute force to optimized: square then sort versus two pointers filling the result from the back.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums sorted in non decreasing order, possibly containing negative numbers, return an array of the squares of every number, also sorted in non decreasing order.

blocks.caption: The largest squares always sit at one of the two ends; fill the result from the back

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums sorted in non decreasing order, possibly containing negative numbers, return an array of the squares of every number, also sorted in non decreasing order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Ranking Distances From Zero on a Number Line
blocks.text: Like a sorted number line where both very negative and very positive numbers can end up far from zero, and squaring collapses that distance into a single positive value, meaning the largest squares always come from whichever end of the line is currently farthest from zero.

blocks.caption: The largest squares always come from one of the two ends of the sorted array

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Squaring every value: 16, 1, 0, 9, 100","sorted ascending","Once squared, the values no longer follow nums' original order; they must be rearranged into ascending order separately"],["Answer","[0, 1, 9, 16, 100]","This is the ascending order of the squared values 16, 1, 0, 9, 100"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Squaring every value: 49, 9, 4, 9, 121","sorted ascending","Two different original values, -3 and 3, happen to square to the same result, 9, and both appear together in the sorted output"],["Answer","[4, 9, 9, 49, 121]","The squared values sorted ascending, including the tied pair of 9s"]]}

blocks.text: With a single value of 0, its square is trivially [0].

Before sorting the squared values from scratch, notice nums itself is already sorted, and squaring does something very specific to a sorted range that spans both negative and non-negative values: it does not preserve order, but it does preserve a predictable shape.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In a sorted array containing both negative and non-negative values, magnitude, distance from zero, does not increase monotonically from left to right; it decreases toward zero and then increases again, a "valley" shape.

Observation 2: Once squared, the largest resulting values can therefore only come from the two far ends of the original array, never from anywhere in the middle, since the middle is exactly where magnitude is smallest.

Observation 3: Comparing the square of the current leftmost remaining value against the square of the current rightmost remaining value, at every step, always correctly identifies which one is the next-largest square overall, since nothing between them could ever be larger.

Observation 4: Filling the result array from its last position backward, placing the larger of the two current end candidates each time and moving that side's pointer inward, builds the fully sorted result in exactly one pass, using the two-pointer structure instead of any comparison-based sort.

Whenever squaring, or any other non-monotonic transformation, turns a sorted range into a "valley" or "peak" shape, the extreme values are always found at the two ends, and two pointers converging from those ends can extract them in the correct order directly.

This is the same "exploit a known shape instead of re-sorting" insight that also justified merging from the back in Merge Sorted Array, just applied here to a valley-shaped transformation instead of a straightforward merge.
Square every value directly, then sort the resulting array from scratch.

items: Square every element of nums.
Sort the resulting array of squares.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The squares are computed independently and in the original array's order, since at this stage no attempt is made to exploit any structure at all.
Sorting is applied to the full list of squares only after every one of them has been computed, since a partial sort would be meaningless before all values are known.
No special handling exists for negative numbers here, since squaring itself already naturally converts any negative value into a positive one before sorting.

blocks.text: Squaring every value and sorting the result is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(n), for the squares array (plus whatever the sort itself needs).

Limitation: the original array is already sorted, and squaring only ever changes the relative order near the boundary between negative and non negative values, information a full sort completely ignores.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Sorting the squared values from scratch throws away a very specific fact: nums was already sorted before squaring, and squaring a sorted range that straddles zero does not scramble it randomly, it folds it into a valley shape, decreasing then increasing in magnitude. That means the same comparison-based work a general sort would do is largely redundant: the two candidates that could possibly be the current largest square are always sitting at the two ends of what remains, never buried somewhere in the middle where a general sort would still have to go looking. Comparing just those two candidates, once per output position, and advancing whichever side loses, replaces an O(n log n) sort with an O(n) single pass, since exactly one comparison decides each output position instead of the many comparisons a full sort performs.

Since the array is sorted, the values with the largest magnitude (farthest from 0) are always found at one of the two ends. Use two pointers starting at both ends, comparing the absolute values (or equivalently the squares) at each end, and placing the larger square into the last remaining slot of the result array, filled from the back, moving whichever pointer produced the larger value inward.
Two pointers from both ends, filling the result array from the back with the larger of the two candidate squares.

blocks.caption: Optimized: two pointers from both ends, filling the result from the back with the larger square

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass filling the result from both ends.
Space: O(n), for the result array, no extra space beyond that.

At every step, the value placed is guaranteed to be the largest square among everything not yet placed, since it is chosen as the larger of the two candidates that could possibly be the largest, the current two ends of the shrinking window; nothing strictly between those two ends could ever have a larger magnitude, since the array is sorted and both ends are moving strictly inward, away from the middle where magnitude is smallest. Filling from the largest position backward to the smallest therefore produces the array in fully correct ascending order by the time the pass completes.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Comparison outcome","Action"],"rows":[["Left candidate's square is larger","Place it at the current back position, then move the left pointer inward (rightward)"],["Right candidate's square is larger or equal","Place it at the current back position, then move the right pointer inward (leftward)"]]}

items: left and right start at index 0 and n minus 1 respectively, the two true ends of the original sorted array, before any values have been placed.

The output loop runs from n minus 1 down to 0, filling the result array from its last index backward, matching the fact that each step determines the next-largest remaining value, not the next-smallest.
Both candidate squares are computed fresh at every step, since either pointer may have moved since the last comparison, changing which value that side currently represents.
Exactly one of the two pointers advances per iteration, never both, since only one value is consumed, placed into the result, at each step.

blocks.text: This problem is a clean example of exploiting sortedness at the two extremes: since squaring is not monotonic across a range that includes both negative and positive values, the two largest-magnitude candidates are always found by comparing the two current ends, never anywhere in the middle.

items: Comparing nums[left] and nums[right] directly instead of their squares, or absolute values, which gives the wrong comparison since a very negative number is smaller in raw value but can have a much larger square.

Filling the result array from the front instead of the back, which would require knowing each value's final position ahead of time, undermining the whole point of building it directly from the largest square down.

Forgetting that the left and right pointers can end up pointing at the same index, an odd-length array with the smallest-magnitude value in the middle, which still needs to be handled correctly as the very last remaining candidate, not skipped.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["An array of all non-negative numbers","The two pointer approach still works correctly, always picking from the right end, the current largest value, until it degenerates to effectively a single pointer scan"],["A single element array","Trivially returns its own square, since left and right both start and immediately end at the same single index"]]}

items: Point out explicitly that the brute force's O(n log n) sort is beaten here specifically because squaring a sorted array is not itself sorted, but is a simple "valley" shape, decreasing then increasing, which two pointers from the ends can exploit directly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "A sorted array transformed by a non-monotonic function, like squaring" points toward thinking about the resulting shape, valley or peak, and whether the two current ends of a shrinking window always hold the next extreme value.

items: What if the array needed to be sorted by descending square instead of ascending? Fill the result array from the front instead of the back, still comparing the two end candidates and placing the larger one first each time.

How would this generalize to any non-monotonic but "unimodal" transformation, one that only changes direction once, not just squaring? The same two-pointer approach from both ends works for any transformation that produces a single valley or peak shape over a sorted input, not specifically x squared.

Could this be done without knowing n in advance, such as a stream? No, the two-pointer approach fundamentally needs both ends of the array accessible upfront; a true single-pass stream would need a different strategy, likely buffering or an entirely different algorithm.
Same "exploit a known shape instead of re-sorting from scratch" insight as Merge Sorted Array's backward merge, just applied to a valley shape instead of two separately sorted halves.
Same "two pointers converging from both ends" structure as Container With Most Water and Valid Palindrome, though the comparison criterion differs in each case.

Same "fill the result from the correct end based on which direction values are being determined" technique reused whenever an output must be built in an order opposite to how candidates are naturally compared.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space (for the output only).

items: Pattern: Two pointers converging from both ends of a sorted array, exploiting the valley shape squaring creates

Core Idea: The largest-magnitude value is always at one of the two current ends of the shrinking window, so filling the result from the back with the larger of the two end squares produces sorted output in one pass
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n), for the output array only
Most Important Observation: A sorted array run through a non-monotonic but unimodal transformation like squaring produces a predictable valley shape, letting two pointers replace a full re-sort
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Biggest square is always at one of the two ends; fill the answer backward
